fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: n=47, p=0.04, -2 Percent
fieldNotes.source: Anonymous growth analyst at Chai Cart, a Gurugram D2C beverage brand
fieldNotes.story:
On September 9, 2024, Chai Cart's marketing team kicked off an A/B test on the homepage hero. Variant A: 'Premium Assam, Brewed Daily.' Variant B: 'Tea Like Your Naani Made.' The test ran for **two days**. n=47 visitors saw A, n=51 saw B. B converted 6 of 51 (11.8 percent), A converted 2 of 47 (4.3 percent). The growth lead ran a chi-square in a Google Sheet, got **p = 0.04**, and Slack-shouted: *"Naani wins! Ship it!"*

On September 12, the team rolled Variant B to 100 percent of traffic — **47,237 visitors** over the next four weeks. Conversion landed at **9.1 percent**. Variant A's historical baseline, before the test, had been **9.3 percent**. The 'winning' headline was costing them about **₹4 lakh a week** in lost revenue against the prior baseline.

The post-mortem on October 17 had three slides. Slide one: the original p-value. Slide two: a power-analysis calculator showing the test would have needed n ≈ 4,700 *per arm* to detect a true 2-point lift with 80 percent power. Slide three, in 60-point font: **"We declared a winner from noise."**

The growth lead now keeps a sticky note above her monitor: *"p < 0.05 ≠ true."* The headline was reverted on October 19.
fieldNotes.takeaway: A small sample with a low p-value is a coin flip wearing a confidence interval. Calculate the n you need before you start, not after you peek.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: The Two-Day Winner
bossBattle.setup:
It's **Week 8**. Aditi has been running her first A/B test — Vyapaar Money's onboarding screen, two variants of a KYC explainer. The PM, Rohan, slides into her DMs at **9:42am on Day 2**: *"Hey Aditi! I peeked at the dashboard. Variant B is up 18 percent, p=0.04. Can we just ship it? Marketing wants to launch the campaign Friday."*

Aditi has 12 hours of data, 312 users in each arm, and a PM with a campaign deadline. She drafts a Slack reply that starts with *"Sure, I think we can—"*. She pauses. She pings you.

coach.name: Staff-DS Sandeep
coach.role: Staff data scientist, has watched seven 'winning' A/B tests revert in production

stages.prompt: Rohan wants to declare a winner at 312 vs 312 users, p=0.04, +18 percent lift. **What's Aditi's first move?**

options.label: "Ship Variant B. p<0.05 is the bar. Don't be the analyst who blocks growth."
options.explain: This is the Chai Cart story word for word. p=0.04 at n=312 with an 18-point claimed lift is almost certainly noise. Aditi will declare a winner that costs the company ₹4 lakh a week. Sandeep is already drafting the post-mortem.

options.label: "Before we declare anything, do a power analysis. What's the minimum detectable effect we actually have power for at n=312?"
options.explain: **Yes.** Aditi runs the calc: at n=312/arm, baseline 8 percent conversion, alpha=0.05, power=0.8 — minimum detectable effect is roughly **+3.4 percentage points**. The observed +1.4 point lift (8 to 9.4 percent) is well below detectable. The 18 percent relative figure is misleading framing of a small absolute move.

options.label: "Just keep the test running for one more week and re-check."
options.explain: Right instinct, wrong rigor. *How long* is the question power analysis answers. 'One more week' is a guess; you need the actual n.

options.label: "Check what the planned sample size was at the start of the test."
options.explain: **Critical.** Sandeep wrote a test-plan template for exactly this. Aditi pulls it up: planned n = 4,200 per arm, planned duration = 14 days. Rohan is asking her to call a winner at 7 percent of the planned sample. The answer writes itself.

stages.prompt: Aditi explains to Rohan: *"We don't have power for this lift size yet."* Rohan replies: *"But the p-value is 0.04! That's significant!"* **How does Aditi respond?**

options.label: "You're right, p<0.05 is the bar. I was overthinking. Shipping."
options.explain: Aditi just got argued out of doing her job. p<0.05 with low power means the *false positive rate conditional on detecting* something is enormous — the 'winning' lift is more likely to be illusion than insight. Sandeep would like a word.

options.label: "p<0.05 controls Type I error at 5 percent IF the test is properly powered. With low power, most p<0.05 results are flukes — and the effect size you see will be inflated. We'd ship a phantom and watch it disappear in prod."
options.explain: **This.** The technical name is 'winner's curse' — under-powered tests systematically inflate effect sizes for the 'winners' you happen to see. Rohan's 18 percent lift, if real, is probably more like 2 to 3 percent. Probably zero.

options.label: "Let's do a Bayesian re-analysis with a skeptical prior."
options.explain: Technically reasonable but a deflection. The PM doesn't need a different statistical framework; he needs to understand why the current evidence is weak. Don't switch tools to avoid a conversation.

options.label: "Let's set a stop rule: continue to planned n=4,200, OR until the lower bound of the 95 percent CI is above zero. Whichever comes first. Document it now."
options.explain: **Operational and rigorous.** Pre-registers the stopping criterion so neither of you is tempted to peek-and-stop. Sandeep nods approvingly from across the office.

stages.prompt: Test runs to planned n=4,200 per arm. Final result: Variant B converts at 8.3 percent vs A at 8.1 percent. Lift = +0.2 points. p = 0.41. **What does Aditi tell Rohan?**

options.label: "Variant B won by 0.2 points but it's not significant. Marketing should still ship it because the direction is positive."
options.explain: 'Not significant but the direction is positive' is how every weak result gets shipped anyway. Either you have evidence or you don't. Aditi just turned a null result into a soft-sell. Sandeep is unhappy.

options.label: "At full power, the lift is 0.2 points and not statistically distinguishable from zero. We can't conclude B is better. The 18 percent we saw at Day 2 was noise — exactly as the power analysis warned."
options.explain: **Clean.** Calls the null result honestly. References the original framing so the team learns from it. This is the analyst Rohan will want on his next test.

options.label: "Result is null. Recommend we test a more aggressive variant — bigger headline, more contrast — and re-run."
options.explain: **Constructive.** Doesn't just deliver a null; suggests the next experiment. The minimum detectable effect tells you how big a difference your test was actually built to find — design the next variant to clear that bar.

options.label: "Result is technically null but if we slice by city tier, Tier-2 users show a +6 percent lift in B with p=0.03."
options.explain: This is the Paisa Vault mistake from Lesson 1, on a Friday. Slicing post-hoc until something hits p<0.05 is exactly the multiple-comparisons trap. Pre-register your subgroups or don't claim them.

outcomes.perfect: You walked Aditi from 'PM wants to ship at Day 2' to a properly powered test with a clean null result and a constructive next step. She shipped nothing she couldn't defend, learned the difference between p-value and power, and Rohan now schedules tests through her. Sandeep buys you both a kulhad chai.
outcomes.good: Most of the instincts are right. The one to drill is the **winner's curse** intuition — that under-powered tests inflate the effect sizes you happen to see, so 'p<0.05 with low power' is worse than no evidence. Re-read the section on power analysis.
outcomes.learn: Aditi shipped a phantom. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **power analysis**, **minimum detectable effect**, and **why early peeking is poison**. Chai Cart reverted in 38 days. You may not be that lucky.
